# Introduction #

This report presents a preliminary exploration of the LA dataset. We conduct various analyses to evaluate surveillance efficacy and the minimal effort required, using the Sepulveda and Eldorado datasets.

# Dataset description #

## Surveillance effort ##

Starting in the late 1988, the dataset includes 161 traps of 6 types (BGSENT, CO2, GRVD, NJLT, USDS, OTHER?) distributed accross 81 sites (trap location) in 2 areas (Sepulveda and Eldorado). Each Trap_ID corresponds to one location and one type of trap. 
Figure \@ref(fig:ActiveSurveillance) illustrates that, until 2004, only 3 NJLT-type traps were set up (2 in *Sepulveda* and 1 in *Eldorado*). Thereafter, significant variation in the number of traps deployed is observed. 

Key observations include:  

- Not all traps have the number of monitored weeks.  

- Monitoring increase after 2003 probably related with **the first detection of West Nile Virus (WNV) in California in 2003** [@reisen_west_2004]. 

- Since 2010, there has been a decline in monitoring effort (Figrue \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear) ). 

```{r ActiveSurveillance, fig.cap="Active surveillance by trap (1 trap is 1 trap type and 1 location) per week in Eldorado (top) and Sepulveda (bottom). Each blue line represents a week during which the trap was active", out.width="80%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/B - ActiveSurveillance.png")

```


### Surveillance effort over years ###

Surveillance efforts have varied over the years and across areas (Figure \@ref(fig:ActiveWeekSurveillance)). The highest surveillance effort occurred around 2005, followed by a decline. Early-season monitoring decreased significantly after 2011, with almost no traps deployed before mid-May in recent years. Since 2005, the number of monitored weeks has been higher in Sepulveda than in Eldorado. 

```{r ActiveWeekSurveillance, fig.cap="Number of weeks with at least one active trap all year around (top), for early season from january to mid may (middle), for late season after mid october (bottom), over monitored weeks", out.width="60%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/B - ActiveWeekSurveillance.png")

```

Figure \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear) shows that the number of traps (each representing a unique location and trap type) set up at least once per year varies significantly, with a sharp increase after 2004. Some traps have been deployed consistently for years, while others have been set up only sporadically (Figure \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear)). 

```{r NtrapsYear, fig.cap="Number of trap set up at least once by year (right) and Number of weeks monitored by each trap (left).",  out.width="45%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center", fig.show="hold", fig.layout="column"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/D - Histogram ntraps by year for selection.png")
knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/D - Histogram traps X nweeks for selection.png")

```

### Surveillance effort by trap type ###

The different types of traps are not used consistently (Figure \@ref(fig:TrappingEffort)). The NJLT trap, deployed in only three locations, was the sole trap type used until 2004 and thus accounted for the highest effort (measured in trap-nights).
After 2004, CO2 and GRVD traps became the main types, deployed across many different locations. In contrast, USDS and BGSENT traps have been used only sporadically.

```{r TrappingEffort, fig.cap="Trapping effort by type of Trap with number of location by trap type (left), number of weeks recorded by trap type (middle) and the total number of trap nights by trap type (right)", out.width="50%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/A - Trapping effort.png")

```


## Mosquito Diversity ##

19 different species has been identified, with *Cx. quiquefasciatus* representing 93% of the total mosquitoes sample (Figure \@ref(fig:HistogramSpecies)).

```{r HistogramSpecies, fig.cap="Proportion of moquitoes species from 1988 to 2022", out.width="50%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/A - Histogram.png")

```

  
## Type of trap impact on species ##

Trap performance for capturing mosquitoes varies depending on species (Figure \@ref(fig:CorrespondenceTable) ). 
Regarding *Cx. quinquefasciatus* only the NJLT trap captures fewer *Cx. quinquefasciatus* than average. This trap type is known to be less efficient at capturing *Cx. quinquefasciatus* [@reisen_comparative_1999]. 
According to the figure, it seems that we observe the general trend only with the CO2 and NJLT traps (except for *Ae. notoscriptus*, captured only once by GRVD).
The "Other" type trap only catches Ae. aegypti — is it a Human-Landing Catch?

```{r CorrespondenceTable, fig.cap="Detection of mosquito species by trap type", out.width="80%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center"}

knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/A - Correspondence table.png")

```

# Surveillance efficacy.  

**Due to a significant change in the monitoring method and the use of only one trap type before 2004, the subsequent analyses are restricted to data from 2004 to 2022 (Figure \@ref(fig:NtrapsYear))**. 

To evaluate surveillance efficacy we fisrt select indicators on which we will evaluate the performance of the surveillance and then try different method of evalutation.
Different methods can be used to evaluate surveillance efficacy. We drew inspiration from a study in New Orleans who has been evaluating different types of traps for monitoring mosquitoes over several years [@scavo_mosquito_2026]. 

Performances indicators :  

- Diversity : alpha-diversity (Shanon) and apparent beta-diversity (Jensen-Shanon). 

- *Culex quinqufasciatus* dynamic : general trend and start season. 

- *Aedes aegypti* : delay in first detection. 

Method of evaluation :

1) **MC indicators** : Using boostraped classical methods : mean value with 5th–95th Percentile Distribution range (Alpha and beta diversity, *Aedes aegypti* : delay in first detection), Spearman correlation rank (*Culex quinqufasciatus* general trend), RMSE (*Culex quinqufasciatus* error in start season). We then just compute 200 randomization by radomly sampling a number a trap to evaluate the impact of the number of traps on the performances indcators. 

2) **Shapley value** : to estimate the importance of each trap (indivually and by trap type) we used the Shapley value. It come from game theory and allow to compute each player (trap) contribution to the outcome (performance). It calculates each player's average marginal contribution across all possible coalitions. Here we present a Monte Carlo adapted version of it (otherwise, it would take way too long) with 10000 permutations.


## Impact on alpha diversity (Shanon). 

Shanon value is relativly low indicating a low diversity. 

### Impact of number of trap on alpha diversity (MC indicators). 

```{r ShannonMC, fig.cap="Impact of the number of trap on Shanon index with in grey the 5th–95th Percentile Distribution Range (MC : 200 reps).", out.width="40%", echo=FALSE, fig.pos = "H", fig.align="center", fig.show="hold", fig.layout="column"}


knitr::include_graphics("Outputs/F - Alpha-biodiversity (Shannon), x-axis nTraps, 200 reps.png")

```

# Perspetives  :

- Explore the impact of trap location (spatial).
- Explore the differences between the two areas. 
- Explore more what has been done in [@scavo_mosquito_2026]. 


# Questions 

- Is it possible to get a update of the data until the end of 2025 ?

- Can we get other datasets from different areas in order to :
  - see if we observe same trend in different locations (same results with a different dataset)?  
  - study the impact of urban green space on vectors. In previous meeting we discussed data from two additional areas : Harbor Lake – Control/ Non-Green (NEW) and Valley Urban – Control/Non-Green. 

- Before 2004 surveillance was very different using only one type of trap, the NJLT. I found in [@reisen_comparative_1999] : *"Originally, light traps were deployed to monitor Cx. tarsalis abundance in relation to enzootic virus transmission activity"*. Do we have specific research question involving data before 2004 ?

-  Performance index and species of interest : so far, we have focused on Shannon diversity index, Shannon-Jensen index, *Cx quiquefasciatus* dynamic and *Ae. aegypti* early detection. 
We need to discuss **species of interest** and **performance index(es)** that can be used.

- The "Other" type trap only catches Ae. aegypti — is it a Human-Landing Catch?
